faq.a: A broad‑spectrum β‑lactam (e.g., ceftriaxone) plus gentamicin, adding metronidazole if anaerobic infection is likely.
faq.q: What is the best empiric therapy for severe sepsis in a HIV‑positive adult?

faq.a: Rely on clinical sepsis criteria, Gram stain if possible, and start locally recommended empiric antibiotics promptly.
faq.q: How do I manage a patient when blood cultures are not available?

faq.a: If the patient has sudden onset diarrhoea with abdominal cramps, no fever, and a history of food exposure, consider Staphylococcus aureus or Bacillus cereus enterotoxins.
faq.q: When should I suspect a toxin‑mediated disease rather than a pure bacterial infection?

exam: A 2‑month‑old infant presents with fever, lethargy and a bulging fontanelle — what immediate investigations and empiric therapy are indicated? — Perform lumbar puncture if safe, start cefotaxime plus ampicillin; assess for meningitis signs.

A patient on chronic dialysis develops a wound infection with purulent discharge; Gram stain shows Gram‑positive cocci in clusters — which organism is most likely and why is vancomycin preferred? — Staphylococcus aureus, high MRSA prevalence in dialysis units; vancomycin covers MRSA.

During a malaria outbreak, a child with sickle cell disease presents with fever and joint pain — which bacterial pathogen should be high on your list and what is the first‑line drug? — Salmonella osteomyelitis; start ceftriaxone.

You receive a sputum sample that is Gram‑negative diplococci; the patient is HIV‑positive with a CD4 count of 150 — what disease does this suggest and what is the recommended treatment? — Neisseria meningitidis meningitis; give ceftriaxone.

A rural clinic lacks culture facilities; a patient with suspected urinary tract infection has a positive dipstick for nitrites — how do you decide on antibiotics? — Treat empirically with nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole, considering local resistance patterns.

A postoperative patient develops wound dehiscence and foul smelling discharge; Gram stain shows mixed anaerobes — what is the key management step? — Initiate metronidazole plus a broad‑spectrum β‑lactam, ensure surgical drainage.

A traveller returns with fever, rash and a history of freshwater swimming; what bacterial infection must be excluded and which test is most useful? — Leptospira interrogans; perform microscopic agglutination test or PCR if available.

In a patient with severe diarrhoea, stool microscopy shows no leukocytes and a rapid test for cholera toxin is positive — what is the mainstay of therapy? — Aggressive oral rehydration; give a single dose of doxycycline if adult and no contraindication.
ai.title: Medical Bacteriology Course Outline
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: A concise guide for fourth‑year students on bacterial pathogens most relevant to low‑resource East African hospitals. It links clinical presentation, limited investigations and pragmatic management to exam expectations.

b: Focus on common Gram‑positive and Gram‑negative organisms, zoonoses and opportunists in HIV/TB patients.
Emphasise bedside reasoning when laboratory support is sparse.
sections.p: Bacteriology teaches how to recognise, investigate and treat bacterial infections that dominate ward caseloads in resource‑limited settings.

b: Cell wall type (Gram stain), capsule, toxin production, and antimicrobial resistance mechanisms.
Growth requirements (aerobic, anaerobic, fastidious) that affect culture availability.
sections.p: Key microbiological traits that influence pathogenicity and choice of empiric therapy.

b: Direct contact, contaminated water, vectors (e.g., flies for dysentery), nosocomial spread via devices.
Reservoirs include humans, livestock, soil and water sources common in tropical regions.
sections.p: How bacteria reach the patient and persist in the community or hospital.

b: Organ‑specific scores: CURB‑65 for pneumonia, MELD for hepatic infection, WHO severe malaria criteria for co‑infection.
High‑mortality pitfalls: meningitis in neonates, necrotising fasciitis, toxin‑mediated shock.
sections.p: Typical clinical syndromes, severity grading and complications to watch for on the ward.
Pragmatic approach to confirming bacterial infection when full labs may be absent.

t.b: Does the sample contain bacteria and what type? Positive stain directs empiric choice; a negative result does not rule out infection.

t.a: Rapid antigen test (e.g., pneumococcal urinary antigen)
t.b: Is Streptococcus pneumoniae present? Positive supports targeted therapy; if unavailable, treat empirically for typical pathogens.
Is there bacteremia and which organism? Guides definitive therapy; if cultures cannot be done, rely on clinical sepsis criteria.

b: First‑line empiric regimens based on local resistance patterns (e.g., ampicillin‑gentamicin for neonatal sepsis).
Switch to narrow‑spectrum agents once organism and sensitivities are known.
Avoid fluoroquinolones in children and pregnant women due to cartilage toxicity.
Implement hand hygiene, safe injection practices and wound care to curb spread.
sections.p: Stepwise management: empiric antibiotics, de‑escalation, supportive care and infection‑prevention measures.

b: Remember the three most common causes of community‑acquired pneumonia in East Africa: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and atypical Mycoplasma.
In a febrile child with sickle cell disease, prioritize Salmonella osteomyelitis over Staphylococcus.
When Gram stain shows Gram‑negative rods in a patient with recent urinary catheterisation, think of ESBL‑producing Enterobacteriaceae.
